transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-10-31
Start: 15:00 UTC
Duration: 00:56:00
Location: Zoom
Attendees: Phil Ramos (Redwood AE), Jenna Cho (Redwood SE), Marcus Lee (Redwood Solutions Eng), Max Chen (Hawthorn CTO), Lara Singh (Hawthorn SRE Lead), Omar Patel (Hawthorn ML Eng), Tina Reyes (Hawthorn Procurement)

Auto-generated summary:
- Hawthorn is evaluating reserved/dedicated capacity for latency-sensitive inference across healthcare datasets; primary concerns are isolation, burst behavior, cost predictability, and compliance (HIPAA).
- Interested in prewarm/warm-pool patterns, failover to hosted, and private VPC option.
- Agreed next step: send sizing/pricing and run benchmark with customer prompts.

Topics: reserved capacity, tenant isolation, warm pools/prewarm, burst strategy, fallback to hosted, VPC/KMS, compliance docs

Transcript body:
[00:00] Phil Ramos: Hey everyone thanks for carving out time today, um quick introductions — I'm Phil, AE on the Dedicated team at Redwood. Jenna's gonna walk through the ops details and Marcus will chime on the benchmarks.
[00:08] Max Chen: Thanks Phil. Max here, CTO at Hawthorn. We run real-time clinical summarization for telehealth sessions so latency is like a hard SLO for us.
[00:15] Jenna Cho: Awesome, thanks Max. Lara and Omar from infra and ML?
[00:19] Lara Singh: Yep Lara here. We're responsible for production infra and compliance.
[00:21] Omar Patel: Omar, ML eng. I'm mostly focused on model latency and tokenization patterns.
[00:24] Tina Reyes: Tina from procurement, nice to meet you all.
[00:27] Phil Ramos: Great. Quick agenda: understand your current infra and constraints, talk about Redwood Dedicated reserved pools and isolation models, prewarm/warm pool options and burst behavior, then pricing/next steps. Sound good?
[00:36] Max Chen: Yes. I'll start with context: we currently self-host on AWS, a mix of EKS for app layer and EC2/GPU instances for inference. We're running a trimmed LLaMA variant — mostly 70B-ish quantized to reduce costs. We have strict PHI handling requirements so data must be encrypted at rest and in transit and we need audit logging.
[00:52] Jenna Cho: Got it. Helpful. Are you shipping inference through an internal endpoint today or via a model serving layer?
[00:57] Omar Patel: We use Triton at the moment in a sidecar pattern and a small homegrown router. It's fine for now but costs spike during booking surges and model warm-up slows tail latency.
[01:08] Jenna Cho: Okay that maps. So two big themes: isolation/commitment for PHI workloads, and burst handling for unpredictable telehealth peaks. Can I walk you through Redwood's reserved capacity models?
[01:18] Max Chen: Please.
[01:19] Jenna Cho: We offer Dedicated reserved GPU pools you can commit to — those are isolated to your account and can be single-tenant nodes or tenant-fenced within a cluster depending on compliance needs. For PHI and HIPAA customers we recommend private VPC + dedicated nodes so the hypervisor and sg boundaries are tighter, and you get KMS-integrated key management.
[01:37] Lara Singh: When you say tenant-fenced, do you mean hardware-level isolation or just software namespaces? We need assurance around noisy neighbor and data plane separation.
[01:45] Jenna Cho: Good question. We have a spectrum: "shared but tenant-fenced" uses strong cgroup and network policies plus NVidia MIG slicing where available, but for full hardware isolation we can provision dedicated instance pools where only your workloads run — that's the single-tenant option. For HIPAA we'd push towards the dedicated option.
[02:01] Marcus Lee: To add — we also support physical tenancy for some enterprise customers that require it; that's a separate contract because of capacity reservation.
[02:08] Lara Singh: Okay that helps. Cost delta? We're sensitive to budget but uptime SLO is top priority.
[02:13] Phil Ramos: We'll share a pricing sheet, but typically dedicated single-tenant pools come at a premium vs shared/tenant-fenced. We work with customers on commit levels so you get predictable unit pricing. For Hawthorn's traffic pattern we can model forecasted token throughput and show a breakeven vs burst egress to hosted.
[02:29] Max Chen: We also need fast cold-start times — telehealth sessions can have first-message latency expectations around 250ms for short prompts. How does Redwood reduce warm-up?
[02:38] Jenna Cho: Two pieces: prewarm/warm pools and KV cache pinning. You can keep a warm pool of pre-initialized workers ready for traffic, and we do prefix/KV caching across sessions which reduces repeated compute. There's also a fast path for quantized kernels. But there is a cost tradeoff: warm pools add steady-state cost vs lower tail latency.
[02:58] Omar Patel: Can you explain how warm pools scale during a surge? Say we have 5x normal traffic for 10 minutes — do you spin up new instances or borrow from a shared pool?
[03:08] Jenna Cho: We do a hybrid. If you're on Dedicated with reserved capacity, we provision buffer capacity — we recommend a "burst guard" commit percentage that you keep unallocated for surges. If demand exceeds reserved + buffer, our routing can fail over to compatible hosted variants in another region or lower-capacity quantized models per your policy. We can also support short-term burst capacity purchases if you expect periodic big events.
[03:30] Max Chen: The fallback to hosted — that concerns us because PHI shouldn't leave our VPC. Is there a private-hosted fallback?
[03:36] Phil Ramos: For PHI workloads we typically recommend a multi-tier policy: primary traffic stays in your dedicated VPC. If you want absolute assurance that nothing leaves, we can disable hosted fallback and instead provision additional reserved on-demand capacity or configure pre-warmed standby nodes. Alternatively, for customers that can tolerate degraded outputs but not data egress, we can route to a lower fidelity variant inside the same private deployment.
[03:57] Lara Singh: KMS integration — is Redwood using our KMS or do we manage keys? We need to keep control of key rotation.
[04:03] Jenna Cho: You manage the KMS; Redwood integrates so encryption at rest uses your keys. We also publish audit logs for key usage and can export them to your SIEM.
[04:12] Omar Patel: About warm-pool sizing — if Marcus runs a benchmark with our prompts, can you recommend the right commit level and buffer?
[04:18] Marcus Lee: Yes — that's exactly what the benchmark is for. We'll ask for representative prompt sets and token length distribution. From that we compute tokens/sec, concurrency needs, and recommended reserved GPUs plus buffer for prewarm.
[04:28] Max Chen: What kind of observability would we get? We need per-token latency, KV cache hit rates, and per-route traces visible to our team.
[04:35] Jenna Cho: Redwood Console provides per-route breakdowns, token-level cost, and tracing hooks. You can export to Datadog/new relic and get granular metrics — we also support per-token billing attribution for teams.
[04:45] Tina Reyes: Procurement question — what's the commitment cadence? Monthly? Annual? Are there penalties for scaling down?
[04:51] Phil Ramos: We have flexible reserved terms — monthly and annual contracts. Early termination is possible but pricing differs. For pilots we often start with a 3-month reserved pilot that converts into a longer-term commit once you hit production usage. We'll put options on the quote.
[05:02] Lara Singh: Network peering — is there a required topology? We want VPC peering and private link.
[05:07] Jenna Cho: VPC peering or PrivateLink both supported. We'll send an architecture diagram with the CIDR expectations and NAT recommendations.
[05:14] Omar Patel: Any limitations on model size or sequence length on the dedicated service? We heavily rely on longer context windows for session summarization.
[05:21] Marcus Lee: We support long-context models; kernel selection optimizes based on sequence length. For very long sequences we may recommend specific model archs or sharded-execution profiles; we'll include those notes in the benchmark report.
[05:33] Max Chen: You mentioned KV cache pinning earlier — can that be persisted across sessions or is it per-worker only?
[05:38] Jenna Cho: We can persist prefix caches for common prompts and share across a warm pool to reduce re-computation; persistence duration is configurable depending on privacy needs. For PHI, you'd likely choose shorter TTLs or not persist across patient sessions.
[05:51] Phil Ramos: Quick callouts: security pack (SOC2/HIPAA), KMS integration, private VPC, single-tenant nodes are all supported. We'll include those artifacts in the follow-up.
[05:59] Tina Reyes: Good. Can you include an estimate for total cost of ownership comparing: (A) our current self-hosted runrate, (B) Redwood reserved single-tenant, (C) Redwood reserved tenant-fenced with fallback to hosted?
[06:10] Phil Ramos: Yes we'll produce a comparative model once we get the prompt sets and basic token metrics — that's part of the sizing spreadsheet.
[06:18] Omar Patel: A couple of practical questions: how do you handle model version pinning and rollbacks? We need stable model behavior during clinical updates.
[06:24] Jenna Cho: We provide model pinning and rollout controls in the Console — canary rollouts, A/B, and automatic fallback to a stable version if we detect quality regressions. We also preserve inference traces for debugging.
[06:35] Max Chen: Anything else we should know about prewarm costs? If we keep a 10-node warm pool 24/7 that's expensive. Any tips for cost control?
[06:42] Marcus Lee: You can use dynamic prewarm based on calendar or traffic prediction, and we have autoscaling that keeps a minimal pool plus predictive warmers. Another approach is hybrid: warm the hot path models and keep a smaller set for heavier, rarer workloads. We'll show a few scenarios in the spreadsheet.
[06:56] Lara Singh: On the compliance docs — what level of evidence do you provide? e.g., do you share penetration test summaries and audit log formats?
[07:02] Phil Ramos: We can share SOC2 Type II summary, penetration test attestations (redacted), and a sample audit log schema. For enterprise agreements we can add custom CLAs and data processing addendums.
[07:12] Tina Reyes: Timeline — if we want to pilot in early December, is that realistic?
[07:16] Phil Ramos: If we get the sample prompts and sizing this week, we can schedule a benchmark the week of 11/12, and spin a pilot environment after the benchmark in late November — early December pilot is feasible.
[07:27] Max Chen: Great. Any gotchas we should watch for during benchmarking?
[07:30] Jenna Cho: Make sure you provide representative concurrency patterns and worst-case prompts (long contexts). Also include a few interactive sessions to measure tail latency.
[07:38] Omar Patel: We'll do that.
[07:40] Phil Ramos: Alright let's recap next steps. Jenna, Marcus and I will send the spreadsheet, prewarm playbook, SOC2/HIPAA docs, and propose benchmark times. Hawthorn will share prompt sets, token distributions, and confirm peering requirements.
[07:52] Max Chen: Sounds good — thanks everyone.
[07:55] Tina Reyes: Thanks all.
[07:58] Phil Ramos: Thanks team, we'll follow up by email with artifacts and proposed times.
[08:02] Call ends.

Notes on transcription quirks: some product names transcribed as "K-V cash" or "Triton sidecar" with minor punctuation oddities; speaker overlap noted at [00:27].
